Interactive demo  ·  illustrative applicant  ·  synthetic data

Some of your best borrowers don't have a credit file to prove it.

This is a short, open-source demonstration of how traditional credit information can be supplemented with everyday financial signals — rent, utilities, cash flow — to produce an assessment a loan officer can actually read, question, and check for fairness. Not a product pitch. A working example, walked through with one fictional applicant.

Walk through the example ↓ View the code on GitHub
The idea in three parts
01

Look beyond the bureau file

With an applicant's consent, weigh rent, utility, and cash-flow patterns alongside — not instead of — traditional credit data.

02

Show the reasoning

Every assessment comes back with plain-language reasons, so a human can see why — not just a score.

03

Check for fairness

Built-in metrics flag when approval rates diverge sharply across groups, so it's monitored rather than assumed.

Walkthrough

Meet the applicant

Six steps, one fictional small business. Steps 3 to 6 use the platform's actual data fields, model, and logic — the assessment, the reasons, and the fairness numbers are live output. Steps 1 and 2 are the situation a loan officer walks in with; the platform never sees them.

Maria's Bakery — working-capital application Fictional example

Applicant profile

Maria has run her bakery for three years. Revenue is steady but seasonal, and — like many small business owners — most of her financial life runs through her business checking account and her landlord, not a credit card.

Business
Maria's Bakery
Structure
Sole proprietor, owner-operated
Time in business
3 years
Requesting
$35,000 working capital
Purpose
Second oven, seasonal demand
What the platform actually scores here is Maria the person, not the bakery as an entity: her rent, her utilities, and the cash flow through her account, used as a proxy for the business. That is how CDFIs and micro-business lenders already underwrite owner-operated borrowers, and it is what this feature set supports today — there is no business-specific contract yet. The amount and purpose above are lender context; the model has no loan-size, term, or debt-to-income input, so this profile would score identically for $5,000 or $350,000.

Traditional credit file

On paper, there isn't much to go on. A thin file like this is common — by some estimates, tens of millions of U.S. adults are considered credit invisible or unscorable using conventional methods alone. It doesn't mean someone is risky. It means the bureau file has little to say.

Credit file status
Thin file
Open trade lines
1 (secured card, opened 4 months ago)
Loan history on file
None
Conventional bureau score
Not yet scoreable
The widely used bureau models need at least one account open for six months or more, so a card opened four months ago does not yet produce a conventional score. Note what this step is and isn't: it is the situation a loan officer faces, not an input to the platform. The model never receives any of the four fields above — it reads only the nine alternative-data fields in the next step.

Additional financial signals

With Maria's consent, the platform can also look at day-to-day financial behavior — the kind of information her landlord and utility provider already have, but a credit bureau doesn't.

These nine values are the complete set the model receives — nothing else from the previous steps reaches it. The rent figure is Maria's home lease, which is the payment record a landlord can verify; the volatility index is a normalised 0–1.5 measure where the reference profile sits at 0.24, so 0.285 reads as mildly seasonal.

Credit assessment

The assessment isn't a yes/no gate — it's a starting point an underwriter can read, question, and combine with their own judgment and policy.

53.7/100
Above the review threshold, with one factor flagged

Read this as a probability of on-time repayment on a 0–100 scale, not as a credit score. For calibration: an applicant sitting exactly on the platform's published reference profile scores 51.8, and the strongest inputs the contract allows reach 81.1. Maria clears the threshold on the strength of her verified income, with one factor flagged for a human to weigh — see the next step.

This is the actual output of the platform's baseline model for this scenario — live-scored against the real API, not staged. That model is trained on synthetic demonstration data only and its baseline ROC-AUC is modest, which is why the scores above cluster near the middle of the range. Treat the number as illustrative of the workflow, not as a production-grade score, and not as a real underwriting decision.

Key factors behind this assessment

Instead of a black-box score, the system returns plain-language reasons — the same kind of information adverse-action notices are meant to convey under fair lending law.

What helped

  • Verified monthly income well above the reference profile — by far the largest positive
  • Three years running the bakery, entered as job tenure
  • Utility payments ahead of the reference on-time rate
  • Rent paid on time every month, though it moves this baseline only slightly

Worth watching

  • Seasonal cash-flow swings — the only reason code the model raised

Neutral: no overdrafts and no NSF events in the past 12 months, and two years at the same address — each sits exactly on the reference profile, so neither helps nor hurts.

An honest reading of the explainability panel further down: on this baseline, income and cash-flow volatility do nearly all the work, and rent history moves the score far less than the premise of this project implies. Dropping Maria's rent from 100% to 50% on time costs about one point and does not change the decision. That is a weakness of a model trained on synthetic data where almost every simulated applicant already pays rent on time — and it is exactly the kind of thing the explanation layer exists to surface. Making rent history carry its weight is open modelling work, listed in the project's own risk register rather than hidden behind the score.

Fairness check

This isn't Maria-specific — it's a portfolio-level check a lender runs on demand against a batch of decisions. Below: selection rate by age group, computed live by the fairness endpoint from the console's built-in monitoring batch.

Ages 18–24 75%
Ages 25–34 75%
Ages 35–44 50%
Gap between highest and lowest group: 25 percentage points — large enough that the metrics came back flagged for review rather than stable. That's the check working as intended: surfacing a signal for a human to look at, not quietly folding it into an approval rate.
Be precise about what this does and doesn't show. The monitoring batch is a fixture: its decisions and outcomes are pre-set in the console so the metrics have something deterministic to measure, and the model did not produce them. The 25-point gap is a property of that fixture, not evidence about this model. When the model does score a real cohort — the 24-application portfolio pass shown further down — the selection rate comes back identical across every age group. Measuring a live model this way needs a lender's own decisions and observed outcomes, which is what the outcome feedback loop is for.

In practice

How a lender might use this alongside existing underwriting

The platform is built to sit next to a lender's process, not replace it.

01

Officer reviews

A loan officer sees the applicant, the assessment, and the plain-language reasons behind it.

02

Weighed against policy

That information is combined with the institution's own underwriting policy, documentation, and judgment.

03

Lender decides

The lending decision — and the compliance responsibility for it — stays with the lender, not the platform.

Scope

What this is — and isn't

This is

  • An open-source framework for alternative-data credit assessment
  • A demonstration environment using synthetic data
  • A way to explore explainable, fairness-aware scoring approaches
  • Something a technical team could pilot, test, or extend

This is not

  • A credit bureau or a production scoring service
  • An automatic approve/deny system
  • A guarantee of improved lending outcomes
  • Currently in use by any financial institution
  • Legal or compliance advice
Under the hood

The full implementation — feature definitions, the scoring API, fairness metrics, and audit logging — is public.
